title: 2 Chronicles 15:8–19
context: Encouraged by the prophecy, Asa removes abominations from Judah, Benjamin, and the captured cities, and repairs the LORD’s altar. People from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon join Judah, seeing that the LORD is with Asa. In Asa’s fifteenth year they gather at Jerusalem, offer sacrifices, and enter a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul, with a penalty of death for any who would not seek him. They swear with rejoicing, the LORD is found by them, and he gives them rest. Asa removes Maacah as queen mother for her Asherah image, though the high places are not taken away out of Israel; his heart is said to be perfect all his days. The parallel for 15:16–18 is 1 Kings 15:13–15. Chronicles dates the end of peace to Asa’s thirty-fifth year, while Kings speaks of war between Asa and Baasha all their days (1 Kings 15:16). Verse 8 speaks of “the prophecy of Oded the prophet,” while 15:1 names Azariah son of Oded; the wording is left as it stands.

verses.text: When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominations out of all the land of Judah and Benjamin, and out of the cities which he had taken from the hill country of Ephraim; and he renewed the LORD’s altar that was before the LORD’s porch.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa takes courage, removes abominations, and repairs the LORD’s altar. Arminian readers note that the prophet’s word moves Asa to action, a clear example of responding to God’s message.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Asa taking courage because God’s word has come to him, so the reform is a response to grace already given.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as renewed reform, with the prophet’s word leading to action at the altar.

verses.text: He gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and those who lived with them out of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon; for they came to him out of Israel in abundance when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa gathers Judah, Benjamin, and people from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon, who come seeing that the LORD is with him. Arminian readers note that people from the north choose to join Judah in worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s presence with Asa drawing others to him, as in 11:13–17. Both traditions read the verse as showing that faithfulness attracts those who also seek the LORD.

verses.text: So they gathered themselves together at Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign.
verses.arminianNotes: They gather at Jerusalem in the third month of Asa’s fifteenth year. Arminian readers note that the date may connect with a feast in the third month, though the text does not name one.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly as a time of covenant renewal for the whole people. Shared ground: both traditions read the dating as historical, without building on a specific festival connection.

verses.text: They sacrificed to the LORD in that day, from the plunder which they had brought, seven hundred head of cattle and seven thousand sheep.
verses.arminianNotes: They sacrifice seven hundred cattle and seven thousand sheep from the plunder. Arminian readers note that the spoil of victory is offered back to God, acknowledging him as the giver of the victory.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the offering as fitting gratitude. Both traditions state the numbers as the text gives them and read the verse as worship arising from God’s deliverance in the war with Zerah.

verses.text: They entered into the covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul;
verses.arminianNotes: They enter a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul. Arminian readers see a solemn, freely made commitment by the people to wholehearted devotion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see covenant renewal as a work of God’s grace among his people. Shared ground: both traditions read the covenant language as echoing Deuteronomy 6:5, with whole-hearted seeking as the response God desires.

verses.text: and that whoever would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman.
verses.arminianNotes: Whoever would not seek the LORD should be put to death, small or great, man or woman. Arminian readers state the provision plainly, noting that it reflects laws such as Deuteronomy 13:6–10 and 17:2–7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse within the setting of Israel as a covenant nation under the law. Shared ground: both traditions report the provision soberly, as narrative about ancient Israel, and neither treats it as a model for today.

verses.text: They swore to the LORD with a loud voice, with shouting, with trumpets, and with cornets.
verses.arminianNotes: They swear to the LORD with a loud voice, shouting, trumpets, and cornets. Arminian readers note the public, joyful character of the oath, made openly before God and one another.
verses.reformedNotes: Loud voices and instruments mark the oath as a festival, and Reformed readers hear covenant gladness in it. Each tradition sees a community binding itself to the LORD together, not a private vow.

verses.text: All Judah rejoiced at the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and sought him with their whole desire; and he was found by them. Then the LORD gave them rest all around.
verses.arminianNotes: All Judah rejoices, having sworn with all their heart and sought him with their whole desire; he is found by them and gives rest. Arminian readers see Azariah’s promise in 15:2 fulfilled in Judah’s experience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s grace in being found and giving rest. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the joyful fulfillment of the prophet’s word, with seeking and finding held together.

verses.text: Also Maacah, the mother of Asa the king, he removed from being queen mother, because she had made an abominable image for an Asherah; so Asa cut down her image, ground it into dust, and burned it at the brook Kidron.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa removes Maacah his mother as queen mother because of her Asherah image, grinding and burning it at the Kidron. Arminian readers note Asa’s courage in confronting idolatry within his own family.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 1 Kings 15:13 records the same act, and that 13:2 names Abijah’s mother differently; the 1 Kings 15 notes discuss the names. Both traditions read the verse as decisive reform.

verses.text: But the high places were not taken away out of Israel; nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect all his days.
verses.arminianNotes: The high places were not taken away out of Israel, yet Asa’s heart was perfect all his days. Arminian readers note that 14:3 and 14:5 say he removed high places; the statements are named, not harmonized.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read “perfect” as wholehearted loyalty rather than sinlessness, as the 1 Kings 15:14 notes do. Shared ground: both traditions note the tension with Asa’s later failures in chapter 16 without resolving it.

verses.text: He brought the things that his father had dedicated and that he himself had dedicated, silver, gold, and vessels into God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Asa brings his father’s and his own dedicated gifts into God’s house. Arminian readers note Asa’s care to honor God with what had been dedicated, completing what his father had begun.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the restoration of the temple’s treasures as part of Asa’s renewal of worship. Both traditions read the verse as parallel to 1 Kings 15:15, closely matching that account.

verses.text: There was no more war to the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign.
verses.arminianNotes: There was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler presents a long period of peace following Asa’s faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 1 Kings 15:16 speaks of war between Asa and Baasha all their days. Shared ground: both traditions name the difference neutrally, and note that the dating here is discussed in connection with 16:1.
